summary: A description of the choices BBN made when implementing the host-host protocol, the initial connection protocol and Telnet on the Terminal IMP. The machine had very little memory and had to drive many different terminals, so some protocol options were chosen to save space and some behaviors do not fully comply with the specifications.

plainLanguage.summary: A tiny computer had to do a big job with very little memory. This note lists the shortcuts its builders took and the rules it does not follow exactly.

subtitle: How Terminal IMP implemented network protocols with severe memory constraints

tldr.problem: Terminal IMPs had only 8 kilobytes of memory to serve 64 terminals, each potentially needing its own network connection. The tight memory budget forced choices about which protocols to implement and how to handle error cases.
tldr.mechanism: The Terminal IMP implemented NCP, ICP, and Telnet but omitted or simplified several protocol features to save memory, such as not guaranteeing correct ECO responses, not handling unsolicited RFCs reliably, and ignoring certain control commands.
tldr.outcome: The Terminal IMP provided network access to terminals but with documented deviations from the full protocol specifications. These practical trade-offs illustrated the tension between protocol compliance and resource constraints.

today: This RFC exemplifies how real-world implementations navigate the gap between protocol ideals and hardware constraints, a challenge that continues in embedded and resource-constrained systems today.

sections.title: The Terminal IMP Architecture
sections.content:
By early December 1971, six Terminal IMPs would be incorporated into the ARPANET to provide network access to terminal users. The Terminal IMP is designed to provide access to the network for its users, not to provide service to other networks.

The machine had no bulk storage for buffering and only 8 kilobytes of 16-bit memory available for both device I/O buffers and program. It needed to drive up to 64 terminals with different types and communication protocols, plus a rudimentary language processor. Since up to 128 simplex network connections could be active at once, each word stored in NCP tables consumed significant memory.
sections.plainLanguage: A small computer box that gives terminals access to the network, but it does not have much memory to work with.

sections.title: Protocol Deviations
sections.content:
The Terminal IMP implements NCP, ICP, and Telnet but has several documented deviations from protocol specifications. It does not guarantee correct response to ECO (Echo) commands if the IMP lacks a free buffer or if its control link is blocked. It does not guarantee to issue CLS (Close) commands for unsolicited RFCs, and it forgets connections after 30 seconds to one minute of waiting for a matching CLS.

The Terminal IMP ignores all RET (Return) commands to avoid infinite RET-ALL loops that would consume bandwidth. It also ignores GVB (Give Back) commands due to implementation complexity. These deviations reflect practical memory and processing trade-offs.
sections.plainLanguage: The small computer skips some rules to save memory and avoid getting stuck in loops with other computers.

sections.title: Design Constraints
sections.content:
Many design choices reflect the Terminal IMP's constraints. It uses simplified allocation handling, ignoring the 32-bit socket number from the Initial Connection Protocol in favor of accepting the first RTS (Request to Send) from the specified host. It treats allocations above 65,534 bits as infinite to store them in a single word, and it limits control messages to 120 bytes.

Socket numbers are preassigned based on terminal hardware addresses rather than being dynamically allocated. During ICP, the Terminal IMP follows the "Listen" option rather than the "Init" option, responding to RFCs rather than initiating them.
sections.plainLanguage: The small computer assigns fixed numbers and rules to save space, letting other computers start conversations instead of starting them itself.

sections.title: Impact
sections.content: These implementation notes documented the practical reality of early network programming: protocol specifications often assume unlimited resources, but real systems must make trade-offs. The Terminal IMP provided valuable network access despite its limitations, and the documented deviations helped other sites understand its behavior and work around it.
sections.plainLanguage: Being honest about what the system can and cannot do helps other people use it correctly.
